analysis.one_liner: Caps medical malpractice payouts at $250,000 and shields FDA-approved drug and device makers from punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 230-194 on July 28, 2005, with 216 of 230 Republicans in favor, but the Senate never voted and the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for medical malpractice lawsuits nationwide. It caps compensation for pain, suffering, and other nonfinancial harm at $250,000, caps punitive damages, shortens the deadlines for filing a claim, caps lawyers' contingency fees, and blocks punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products were approved by the FDA. Supporters said this would lower malpractice insurance premiums and health care costs; opponents said it would leave severely injured patients unable to collect fair compensation.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers would pay out less in lawsuits, and the bill's stated purpose was to lower malpractice insurance premiums and reduce 'defensive medicine' [S2]. Drug and device makers would gain the most sweeping protection: no punitive damages for an FDA-approved product, and doctors who prescribe or dispense such products could not even be named in a product liability suit [S4]. Plaintiffs' lawyers, who take malpractice cases on contingency, would face fee caps that make many cases uneconomical to bring [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Doctors, malpractice insurers, drug and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages — payment for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life — at $250,000 per injury, regardless of how many parties are responsible, and prohibits the jury from being told about the cap [S3].

Allows punitive damages only on clear and convincing evidence of malicious intent or deliberate disregard, caps them at $250,000 or twice economic damages, and prohibits them entirely against makers of FDA-approved medical products except in cases of fraud or bribery of FDA officials [S3].
Shortens the filing deadline to one year after the patient discovers the injury or three years after it manifests, whichever comes first [S3].
Caps attorneys' contingency fees on a sliding scale from 40% down to 15% of large recoveries, and lets courts redirect settlement money away from lawyers [S4].
The bill's stated purpose is to reduce liability costs, lower malpractice insurance premiums, reduce 'defensive medicine,' and improve patient access to care [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Patients hurt by medical negligence. The $250,000 cap falls hardest on people with small economic losses — children, retirees, stay-at-home parents — whose main recoverable harm is the injury itself. Punitive damages would be nearly out of reach, deadlines for suing would shrink, and juries would not be told the cap exists when they decide what a case is worth [S3].

drawbacks.text: A flat $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages undercompensates the most seriously injured patients, and the bill bars juries from being told the cap exists so they cannot factor it into their award [S3].

Drug and device makers whose products were approved by the FDA could not be hit with punitive damages unless a patient proved the company lied to the FDA or bribed an official — a nearly impossible burden for a family harmed by a dangerous drug [S4].
The one-year-from-discovery deadline would end some valid claims before patients even understand what went wrong [S3].

Supporters' honest case: the bill did preserve unlimited recovery of economic damages — lost wages and medical bills — and its proponents argued malpractice litigation raised insurance premiums and health costs for everyone [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is real but lopsided. If lower premiums had materialized and been passed to patients, everyone would share some benefit. But the bill's concrete mechanisms — a hard damages cap, near-impossible punitive damages, an FDA-approval shield, and lawyer fee caps — take money and leverage directly away from injured patients and give it to insurers, providers, and drug makers, with no guaranteed mechanism ensuring any savings reach patients' pockets.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it along mostly party lines, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never took it up, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 230-194 on July 28, 2005; 216 of 230 Republicans voted yes while 184 of 202 Democrats voted no [S7].
Debate was held under a rule that closed the bill to amendments, and a Democratic motion to send it back to committee with instructions failed 193-234 just before final passage [S6].
The Senate received the bill on July 29, 2005 and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which took no further action for the rest of the Congress [S6].
The bill never received a Senate vote and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients kept the full protections of their state laws, including uncapped noneconomic damages where states allow them, and malpractice insurers, physicians, and drug makers did not get the federal caps they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients, who kept full state-law rights

for.name: Rep. Phil Gingrey
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce / Judiciary
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 21, 2005 and shepherded it to House passage within a week.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.role: Reported the rule for floor consideration
for.what_they_did: Reported H. Res. 385, which allowed only two hours of debate and closed the bill to all amendments.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Made limiting medical malpractice lawsuits a high-profile legislative priority throughout 2005, pressing Congress to pass caps on damages.

for.name: American Medical Association and physician groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for national damage caps, citing rising malpractice insurance premiums.

against.name: Rep. John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee with instructions; the motion failed 193-234.

against.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on July 29, 2005 and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Trial lawyers' organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed national damage caps, arguing they strip compensation from patients injured by negligent care.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party: 216 of 230 Republicans voted yes while only 14 of 202 Democrats did; the failed motion to recommit was nearly the reverse, with 192 of 202 Democrats in favor and no Republicans [S7].

industries.note: Damage caps and fee limits directly reduce what insurers must pay on claims, and the bill's stated purpose is to lower the premiums doctors pay them. Their gain comes out of the compensation available to injured patients.

The bill bars punitive damages against any FDA-approved product and prohibits naming prescribing doctors in product suits, leaving a company exposed only if a patient proves it lied to the FDA or bribed an official — a very high bar.

Doctors would face lower liability exposure and, per the bill's stated purpose, lower malpractice premiums. The bill's supporters argued this improves access to care, while opponents noted it also reduces patients' recourse against negligent care.
Sliding-scale fee caps and a $250,000 damages ceiling make many malpractice cases uneconomical to take, shrinking the practice area. Their loss tracks patients' loss of representation in these cases.

The bill bars health plans from recouping payments from a patient's award, but a non-binding 'sense of Congress' provision states health insurers should be liable when their coverage decisions harm patients; neither provision carries legal force.
